power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.formatted: When individuals who used neither nicotine nor cannabis were segregated into groups that also did not use alcohol or used only alcohol, the effect of substance use on total MCSI symptom score remained significant (F 4,685 = 5.04, mean square error (MSE) = 163.40, p < .001, η² = .029).
table.expanded: When individuals who used neither nicotine nor cannabis were segregated into groups that also did not use alcohol or used only alcohol, the effect of substance use on total MCSI symptom score remained significant (F 4,685 = 5.04, mean square error (MSE) = 163.40, p < .001, η² = .029).

table.formatted: Amongst participants that used neither nicotine nor cannabis, post-hoc tests found no difference between those that did not vs. those that did use alcohol (did not use alcohol estimate = 19.61, used alcohol estimate = 20.31, mean difference = -.70, standard error (SE) = 2.13, p > .99).
table.expanded: Amongst participants that used neither nicotine nor cannabis, post-hoc tests found no difference between those that did not vs. those that did use alcohol (did not use alcohol estimate = 19.61, used alcohol estimate = 20.31, mean difference = -.70, standard error (SE) = 2.13, p > .99).
When alcohol use was included an additional factor in mixed models, no effect of alcohol use was observed (F 1,685 = 1.51, MSE = 163.62, p = .22, η² = .002).
The interaction effect between nicotine/cannabis use and alcohol use was also nonsignificant (F 3 ,682 = .33, MSE = 163.62, p = .81, η² = .001).

table.formatted: A significant main effect of cannabis/nicotine use frequency and MCSI total symptoms was observed (F 4,673 = 6.19, MSE = 161.53, p < .001, partial η² = .04).
table.header: Symptom Profiles based on Cannabis/Nicotine Use Frequency
table.expanded: A significant main effect of cannabis/nicotine use frequency and MCSI total symptoms was observed (F 4,673 = 6.19, MSE = 161.53, p < .001, partial η² = .04).

table.formatted: The planned linear contrast of frequency of use relationships (use none < use nicotine-only or cannabis-only less than daily < use nicotine-only or cannabis-only daily < use both but did not use both daily < use both daily) was also significant (linear contrast estimate = 6.45, 95% CI = 3.26 -9.65, p < .001).

table.header: Frequency of Use for Individuals with Co-Use vs. Single Substance Use
table.expanded: Amongst the 175 individuals using nicotine who also had frequency of use data available, no difference was found between nicotine only users vs. individuals who used both nicotine and cannabis in nicotine use frequency (χ2 = .022, p = .88).

table.header: Frequency of Use for Individuals with Co-Use vs. Single Substance Use
table.expanded: Similarly, amongst the 179 individuals using cannabis and who also had frequency of use data available, no difference was observed between those who used cannabis only and those who used both nicotine and cannabis in cannabis use frequency (χ2 = .91, p = .34).

*Significant difference (p < .05, Sidak-corrected).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p > .99", "p < .05"), Text = c("Amongst participants that used neither nicotine nor cannabis, post-hoc tests found no difference between those that did not vs. those that did use alcohol (did not use alcohol estimate = 19.61, used alcohol estimate = 20.31, mean difference = -.70, standard error (SE) = 2.13, p > .99).", 
"*Significant difference (p < .05, Sidak-corrected).")), row.names = c(NA, 
-2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > .99", "p = .22", "p = .81", "p = .88", "p = .34", "p = .35"), Sentence = c("Amongst participants that used neither nicotine nor cannabis, post-hoc tests found no difference between those that did not vs. those that did use alcohol (did not use alcohol estimate = 19.61, used alcohol estimate = 20.31, mean difference = -.70, standard error (SE) = 2.13, p > .99).", "When alcohol use was included an additional factor in mixed models, no effect of alcohol use was observed (F 1,685 = 1.51, MSE = 163.62, p = .22, η² = .002).", "The interaction effect between nicotine/cannabis use and alcohol use was also nonsignificant (F 3 ,682 = .33, MSE = 163.62, p = .81, η² = .001).", "Amongst the 175 individuals using nicotine who also had frequency of use data available, no difference was found between nicotine only users vs. individuals who used both nicotine and cannabis in nicotine use frequency (χ2 = .022, p = .88).", "Similarly, amongst the 179 individuals using cannabis and who also had frequency of use data available, no difference was observed between those who used cannabis only and those who used both nicotine and cannabis in cannabis use frequency (χ2 = .91, p = .34).", "When SES was added as a factor to a model predicting MCSI total score based on nicotine/cannabis use, the SES effect was non-significant (F 2, 615 ) = 1.06, MSE = 163.30, p = .35, η² = .00)." )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
